title: 145. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Testing a Proportional Model from a Graph
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Identifying a Proportional Model from a Straight Line Through the Origin
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a graph supports the proportional model \(y=kx\).
questions.question: A graph of \(y\) against \(x\) is a straight line that passes through the origin. Which model does this graph support?
questions.explanation: A proportional relationship has equation \(y=kx\), and its graph is a straight line passing through \((0,0)\). Since the given line passes through the origin, it supports the proportional model \(y=kx\). Option A includes a nonzero intercept, which would not pass through the origin.
questions.hint: Check both straightness and the intercept.

questions.concept: Testing Proportionality Using Points on a Graph
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether points on a straight-line graph through the origin support a proportional model.
questions.question: A graph of \(y\) against \(x\) is a straight line through the origin and passes through \((2,6)\) and \((5,15)\). Which conclusion is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It supports a proportional model because \(\frac{y}{x}=3\) for both points.

options.label: B
options.text: It does not support a proportional model because the points have different \(x\)-values.

questions.explanation: For a proportional model, \(\frac{y}{x}\) must be constant. Here, \(\frac{6}{2}=3\) and \(\frac{15}{5}=3\). The graph is also a straight line through the origin, so it supports \(y=3x\). Option B is incorrect because different \(x\)-values do not prevent proportionality.
questions.hint: A proportional line uses its slope as the constant.

questions.concept: Recognizing a Non-Proportional Graph with a Nonzero Intercept
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a straight-line graph that does not pass through the origin supports a proportional model.
questions.question: A graph of \(y\) against \(x\) is a straight line passing through \((0,2)\) and \((4,10)\). Does it support the proportional model \(y=kx\)?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the graph is a straight line.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the graph does not pass through the origin.

questions.explanation: A proportional graph must pass through the origin. This line has \(y=2\) when \(x=0\), so it does not pass through \((0,0)\). Therefore, it does not support the model \(y=kx\). Option A only checks straightness, which is not enough.
questions.hint: Use a given point to test the proportional model.

questions.concept: Finding the Constant of Proportionality from a Graph
questions.learningObjective: Determine the constant of proportionality from a point on a proportional graph.
questions.question: A graph of \(y\) against \(x\) is a straight line through the origin and passes through \((3,12)\). What is the constant of proportionality \(k\) in \(y=kx\)?
questions.explanation: For a proportional graph, \(k=\frac{y}{x}\). Using the point \((3,12)\), \(k=\frac{12}{3}=4\). Therefore, the constant of proportionality is \(4\). Option B is the \(x\)-value, not the constant.
questions.hint: For a line through the origin, divide the \(y\)-coordinate of a point by its \(x\)-coordinate.

questions.concept: Testing Proportionality from Multiple Graph Points
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a set of points on a graph supports a proportional model by checking constant ratio.
questions.question: A graph contains the points \((1,2)\), \((2,5)\), and \((3,8)\). Does it support a proportional model?
questions.explanation: Check the ratios: \(\frac{2}{1}=2\), \(\frac{5}{2}=2.5\), and \(\frac{8}{3}\approx 2.67\). The ratios are not equal, so the points do not lie on a proportional line \(y=kx\). Option A confuses increasing values with proportionality.
questions.hint: A proportional line uses its slope as the constant.

questions.concept: Using Slope of a Proportional Graph
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a value from the slope of a proportional graph.
questions.question: A graph of a proportional model \(y=kx\) is a straight line through the origin with slope \(0.5\). What is \(y\) when \(x=10\)?
questions.explanation: In a proportional graph, the slope is the constant \(k\). Here \(k=0.5\), so \(y=0.5\times 10=5\). Therefore, \(y=5\). Option A incorrectly doubles the value.
questions.hint: In \(y=kx\), the slope is \(k\); substitute the given \(x\)-value.

questions.concept: Criteria for Testing a Proportional Graph
questions.learningObjective: Identify the graph features required to support a proportional model.
questions.question: When testing whether a graph supports a proportional model, which feature must be verified?

options.label: A
options.text: The line has a positive slope only.

options.label: B
options.text: The graph is a straight line passing through the origin.

questions.explanation: A proportional model \(y=kx\) has a graph that is a straight line through the origin. A positive slope alone is not sufficient, because a line with positive slope could still have a nonzero intercept. Therefore, the required feature is a straight line through the origin.
questions.hint: Check both straightness and the intercept.

questions.concept: Predicting a Value from a Proportional Graph
questions.learningObjective: Use a point on a proportional graph to predict another value.
questions.question: A proportional graph \(y=kx\) passes through \((4,10)\). What is \(y\) when \(x=6\)?
questions.explanation: The slope is \(\frac{10}{4}=2.5\), so the requested value is \(2.5\times 6=15\). The alternative \(12\) adds the coordinate increase to the old output, \(10+(6-4)=12\), rather than scaling.
questions.hint: A proportional line uses its slope as the constant.

questions.concept: Testing a Linear Graph with a Nonzero Intercept
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a linear equation with a nonzero intercept represents a proportional model.
questions.question: A straight-line graph is described by \(y=2x+3\). Does it support the proportional model?
questions.explanation: A proportional model has the form \(y=kx\), whose graph passes through the origin. The line \(y=2x+3\) has \(y\)-intercept \(3\), so it does not pass through \((0,0)\). Therefore, it does not support a proportional model. Option A only considers the slope.
questions.hint: Use a given point to test the proportional model.

questions.concept: Comparing Constants of Proportionality from Graphs
questions.learningObjective: Determine which proportional graph has the larger constant of proportionality.
questions.question: Graph A is a proportional line through the origin with slope \(3\). Graph B is a proportional line through the origin with slope \(2\). Which graph has the larger constant of proportionality?
questions.explanation: For a proportional graph \(y=kx\), the constant of proportionality is the slope. Graph A has slope \(3\), and Graph B has slope \(2\). Since \(3>2\), Graph A has the larger constant. Option B is incorrect because \(2<3\).
questions.hint: Relate the constant of proportionality in \(y=kx\) to a feature of the line.
